description: We translate raw ideas into binary reality. Composed of passionate developers, architects, and problem-solvers, Zeroes and Ones is built to bridge the gap between complex algorithms and seamless digital experiences. Fueled by rapid prototyping, clean code, and a obsession with performance, we are here to build, scale, and ship a high-impact solution before the clock runs out.
summary: Trend Detective is a free, open-source web app that answers one question: is this part of Earth really changing, or is it just noise? You pick one of 15 NASA variables (temperature, rainfall, vegetation, haze, sea ice, sea level and more), then a season and a place. It shows what is changing, where, by how much, and whether the change is statistically significant. It uses 23 years of real NASA satellite data (2003–2025). It corrects for two common traps: back-to-back years are not independent, and testing thousands of map cells at once flags some by pure chance. Its main lesson is “same variable, opposite story”: the same measure can rise in one region and fall in another. We checked it against published science, and 6 of 7 checks pass.
details:
What it does
Trend Detective turns NASA Earth data into evidence that anyone can check. There are three choices: a “clue” (one of 15 variables), a season (the full year or one of four seasons) and a place (23 sites, from the Arctic to the Indo-Gangetic Plain). The app maps the trend and tests it. Each site has a plain-language case file covering what is happening, why it matters and the key facts. A time machine steps through the years, and turning-point detection shows when a trend changed direction. One click downloads a CSV with the yearly values, the trend, the data source and a citation.

How it works
A Python pipeline pulls data from NASA’s Common Metadata Repository. Where it can, it downloads only the variables it needs, which turns a 22 GB dataset into about 0.2 GB. It puts every dataset on the same 0.5° monthly grid covering January 2003 to December 2025 (276 months). For each map cell and region it calculates a Sen slope and a Mann-Kendall significance test. We ran a simulation to compare five testing methods and chose a variance-corrected version. It raised false alarms 8% of the time, against 21% for the standard test, and still found 76% of real trends. A false-discovery-rate correction keeps thousands of simultaneous tests from lighting up the map by chance. The web app runs as a static site on GitHub Pages and is built with React, TypeScript and MapLibre.

Why it matters
Climate claims are everywhere, but students and the public rarely get to test one. Trend Detective shows that “not significant” means “not proven”, not “no change”. It also shows when a straight-line trend is the wrong tool. For example, haze over eastern China rose until about 2011 and then fell, so a single line through the whole period hides both halves.

Scientific honesty
We kept the checks that don’t fully pass instead of tuning them until they did. When a sensor gave wrong results, we switched to a better source:

  • Terra’s orbit drift made land temperatures look too cold, so we moved to the Aqua satellite.
  • OMI’s sensor fault created a fake ozone rise, so we moved to OMPS.
  • The GLDAS model showed global soil drying that other sources didn’t confirm, so we moved to ESA’s CCI soil-moisture data.

Our results match published records. September Arctic sea ice falls 11.56% per decade (NSIDC reports 11.6%). Global temperature rises 0.275 °C per decade (NASA’s GISTEMP gives the same figure). Greening in China and India and cooling of the upper atmosphere also match.

Data

  • NASA: GISTEMP v4, MODIS (NDVI, land surface temperature, snow cover, sea surface temperature, chlorophyll), GRACE/GRACE-FO, MERRA-2, GPM IMERG, NSIDC sea ice, OMI NO₂, OMPS ozone, AIRS and NASA-SSH sea level.
  • Space Agency Partners: ESA’s CCI Soil Moisture. GPM, the source of our rainfall data, is a joint NASA–JAXA mission.

Quality
Every code change is tested automatically. The checks cover 41 tests of the statistics code, tests of the web app, full browser walkthroughs and a WCAG 2.1 AA accessibility check.

Tools: Python, NumPy, React, TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre, Playwright, GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages. The code is MIT-licensed.
